content.content:
# The report and the record

## What every report holds

Your brief says where your report goes: a file that it names, your final message, or both. If it names no file, your report is your final message.

A finding is something that your work learned about the tree or the language, and that the record does not hold yet. Examples: a defect, a behaviour that departs from the specification or from a decision of the curator, a measurement. What you did along the way is not a finding, for example the files that you read or edited. Your transcript keeps that.

A fact is a finding that is an established property of the tree, the language, the library or their tools, and that later work builds on. A defect also gets its ledger row, and a fact about it may cite the row.

A point to report is a kind of change or finding that the curator wants to review. Your brief names its points to report. Examples: a changed line of a test that the team wrote, a checker edit inside a change to the library, a changed line of the model program.

Put each of these that you have in your report, in this form, whatever else your brief asks for:

- **Defects.** Each defect that you measured, and the test or ledger row that records it (`tests-writing.md`, "How a defect is recorded").
- **Sentences of the specification made false.** Each sentence of the specification that your change makes false, quoted with its file and line. Such a sentence says what walk or the compiled path does. It is in the effect of an Appendix I entry (`Specification/appendices/changes.tex`), or in a `\revision` or `\note{}` box beside a passage.
- **Decisions.** Each choice that you made among alternatives, as a decision apart from the findings: what you chose, the alternatives, and the evidence, cited. If no decision of the curator covers it, say so, and say which reading you acted on. A decision left as a line inside the findings counts as not made.
- **Points to report.** Each point that your brief names and the work reached, with its evidence, also one that only part of the work reached.
- **For FACTS.** Each fact that your work established, in the hand-over form of "Writing to the record". If your brief let you write FACTS, give instead the number of each entry that you added or rewrote. If your work established no fact, write "none".
- **Commands.** Each command that you had to work out because this skill does not give it, with what it does.
- **Questions for the curator.** If something needs the curator's decision, list it as a decision not taken, in the form that `exploring.md` gives. The reader of your report brings it to the curator. Do not choose which of your items anyone reviews.

## At a point to report

- If the work reaches a point to report, do what the brief says for it. For example, a brief can say that a defect in the code is recorded in a ledger row and not repaired.
- Then finish the work.
- If a step cannot be undone, or would change a decision of the curator, report it instead. List it as a decision not taken, with its alternatives.

## Timings and citations

- If you take a timing that you will keep, run nothing else beside it. All agents of the session share the machine's cores (the `cloud-container` skill).
- Name the machine with every timing: `nproc`, the CPU's model and MHz, the load at start, the JDK, `FORTRESS_THREADS`. Only a pair of timings taken in one run measures a difference.
- If you take a measurement again because the code changed, say what changed.
- In a report, cite the tree at file:line, and quote results, two to five lines, each with its command. Never cite a file under `tmp/`.

## POSITIONS and FACTS

POSITIONS and FACTS describe the present: no dates, no names of who found what, no "corrected" or "superseded" notes. The history of each entry is in `POSITIONS-history.md` and `FACTS-history.md`, beside them. When your work needs the detail of an entry, print the report section that it cites (`$T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'`, below). Read its history only when the tree disagrees with the entry.

Each entry is one line that starts with its permanent number: `F-87` in FACTS, `P-48` in POSITIONS. A FACTS entry is the fact as it stands now, what it means for the work, and the test that fails if the fact stops holding, under a bold title. If no test checks the fact, the entry gives the command and the output that show it. It points to the report section that holds the detail. Cite an entry by its number. If the reader must know what the entry says without printing it, add the first words of its title in quotes: F-87, "The first words ...".

## The gap ledger

The ledger's rows are the bug reports that the work fixes. A fix of a row starts with its reproduction, written as a test (`tests-writing.md`).

A row is one line of eight cells, at most 1,200 characters, in the table of a topic section. Reports cite a row by its number, which it keeps for good. A new issue gets a new row.

- Its status is one of seven words: `POSITIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-BOUNDED`, `CONTESTED`, `RETIRED`, `FIXED`, `DUPLICATE`. The last three close a row. The row template (below) defines each.
- Its class is a kind and an area, such as `implementation gap (checker)`.
- The earlier text of a changed row is in `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger-history.md`.

Read the ledger only through the queries below: it is too large to read whole.

A row states its gap as it stands now. A note adds a fact. If your work changes what a row says, write the row's whole new line with `rewrite` (below), not a note that tells the repair.

The heading reader of `ledger.py` does not expand the specification's `\Trait{X}` macro. So a row that names a library trait's section cites `Specification-1.0-frozen/` by line.

## Reading the record

Read only the slice of the record that you need. This tool prints whole entries, in parts of bounded size:

    T=explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh

- `$T 'F-87'` prints one entry by its number, and `$T 'P-48'` one of POSITIONS. `$T 'F-87+'` adds each entry that F-87 cites by its number, and each entry that cites F-87. `$T 'history:F-87'` prints its history. Run one when your brief or a note cites an entry by its number.
- `$T 'positions:WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints one of the curator's decisions. Run it before you choose among ways to do something. If several titles hold the words, it names them.
- `$T 'WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints each FACTS entry whose bold title holds them, and `$T 'section:HEADING'` every entry of a FACTS section. Run one before you investigate a behaviour of the tree, and when your brief or a note names an entry. These queries and `positions:` read titles only: before you write that the record does not hold something, also grep FACTS and POSITIONS for its words.
- `$T 'index:WORDS'` prints the INDEX lines that hold the words. Run it to find the notes on a topic.
- `$T 'ledger-find:WORDS'` prints one line for each ledger row that holds every word. Run it when you meet a defect, before you investigate it.
- `$T 'ledger:ROW'` prints one row whole. Run it for each row that you need from a find, your brief or a note.
- `$T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'` prints a section of any note, or of a `.tex` chapter, and `$T 'map:FILE#HEADING'` a section of a note under `explorations/coordinator/map/`. Run one when your brief or a note names a section. `#HEADING@WORDS` prints only the table rows and list items of that section that hold every one of WORDS.
- `$T --check QUERY ...` prints only where each query matches and its size. Run it before a query whose size you do not know. `--part N` prints part N of a long output, and `--help` gives the rest.

A word of a query that ends in `*` matches the start of a word. Any other word matches a whole word.

Before you edit a file of the original tree, list the ledger rows that cite it, and read each row that your edit can change:

    python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py find --cites FILE

## Writing to the record

- Write FACTS and POSITIONS only with `explorations/coordinator/tools/record.py`, never by hand. `add` gives a new entry its number, and `set` rewrites an entry. The tool writes the entry to `FACTS.md` or `POSITIONS.md`, and its earlier text to the history file beside it. It commits nothing: commit both files in one commit. Its header gives its usage.
- If your brief lets you write FACTS, add each fact as a new entry in the section of its topic, in the commit that establishes it. Put its detail in a section of your report: the file:line citations, the commands with their output, and the measured numbers. Point the entry to that section, by your report's file and the section's heading. If your report is only your final message, hand the fact over instead. Spend no effort on the entry's wording: it is rewritten to the record's form after your work.
- If your brief does not let you write FACTS, hand each fact over in the "For FACTS" item of your report, with:
  - the fact as it stands now, in one sentence;
  - what it means for the work;
  - the number that a decision rests on, if any, with what it counts; if its parts belong to different ledger rows, the part of each row;
  - the test that fails if the fact stops holding, or the command and the output that show it;
  - the section of your report that holds the detail.
- If your brief lets you write FACTS, rewrite a wrong entry in place. Otherwise say in your hand-over that the entry is wrong, with the evidence.
- POSITIONS holds each of the curator's decisions, in one place. Everything else points there. Write a decision there only if your brief gives it to you to record. If you have evidence against one, do as `exploring.md` says.
- Put new files of the work under `explorations/`. If you add a note directly in `explorations/` or `explorations/reviews/`, add its line to INDEX: ``- `PATH`: `` and the first sentence of the note's header comment.

Write the gap ledger only with `ledger.py`, which checks each line that it writes against the row template.

    L="python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py"

To add a row:

1. Print the row template, about 3 KB: `$T 'doc:explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md#The row template'`.
2. Write the row as one line in a file under your tree's `tmp/`, with `?` in its number cell.
3. Run `$L add FILE --section TITLE`. It numbers the row and puts it in that section. If the row breaks the template, it adds nothing and prints each rule broken. `$L sections` lists the titles.

To change a row:

- `$L note N TEXT` adds TEXT to the notes of row N. It refuses a note that takes the row past 1,200 characters, or its notes cell past 700 characters. `$L note N TEXT --check` writes nothing. It says whether TEXT fits, and how many characters the notes and the row have left now and would have left with TEXT. These counts include the separator that the tool adds. It exits 0 if TEXT fits, and 1 if not. Run it before a long note, or before a note on a row near its limits. If TEXT does not fit, shorten it, or cut the notes with `rewrite` (below).
- `$L rewrite N FILE` replaces row N with the whole line in FILE, a file under your tree's `tmp/`, with N or `?` in its number cell. Use it to correct the claim, cut the notes or change the reproducer. The tool checks the line against the template and keeps the old line in the history file.
- `$L duplicate N --of M` makes row N a pointer to row M.
- `$L close N --commit HASH --test NAME` marks row N `FIXED`, by the commit HASH and its test NAME. Run it once that commit is in `HEAD`, and commit the close after it. NAME can also be a file under `explorations/coordinator/tools/`, or `none` with `--note REASON`. For a `CONTESTED` row, add `--settled TEXT`, which names what settled its question.
- `$L landing-check BASE` prints each problem, and exits 1 on any. Run it when your brief asks for it. It checks the whole ledger against the template, so a broken row that BASE already had counts too. The problems are a row that breaks the template, an `XXX` test deleted or renamed while a row that is not closed names it, a row that is not closed though a commit says it fixed it, and a FACTS or POSITIONS entry that disagrees with a row's status.

## The repository's history

- The repository is a 2018 fork of `sirinath/fortress`, a git conversion of the project's java.net Mercurial repository. Its trunk runs from 2007-01-04 to 2012-08-31 and ends at `a874948ac`, the team's last commit.
- The commits after `a874948ac` are the revival's. After the tag `sealed-tree`, commit `75cca6683`, the revival began to fix the team's code, test first. Before it, the revival changed mainly the build and the toolchain.
- `git diff a874948ac -- FILE` shows what the revival changed in a file, and `git diff 75cca6683 -- FILE` what it changed after the tag.
- If the commands above fail, run `git rev-parse --is-shallow-repository`. It prints `true` in a shallow clone, where these commits do not resolve. There, a copyright header of Sun Microsystems or Oracle, as in `Library/Format.fss`, marks a file that the team made, but not which of its lines the port or the revival changed. If your task needs those lines, say in your report that the clone is shallow.
- The conversion cut 146 parent links, so a `git log` of a directory stops at a cut and misses the team's earlier commits. Use `git log --follow` on a file, or compare contents.
- To find who wrote something, or where the repository's history after 2012 comes from, read `research/authorship.md` and `explorations/coordinator/lineage.md`.
- Commit `8fe1daa8f` copied a third-party port of the tree to Java 9 onto the team's last commit, `a874948ac`. Give its lines no credit, and name no author of it in any text that you commit. In a reconstruction of authorship, attribute nothing of it to anyone.

# Keeping the record

How workers read the record, and edit it when a brief asks, is `fortress-repo`'s records part.

**history**
: `FACTS-history.md` or `POSITIONS-history.md`. Under each number, one block per change: a provenance line (the time, the kind of change, the report section, the commit, who, why) and the line as it stood before.

**pointer**
: Another entry's number in the sentence that needs it, with a few words on its subject: "It builds P-48, on a type parameter that a call does not fix."

**pass**
: Your rewrite of what a worker wrote into entries of the form below.

## What an entry is

An entry reads on its own. A reader who knows the language, or can look it up in the `fortress-repo` skill, can tell what it says without the conversation or the batch behind it. The entry lets a worker or you act right without opening the report, and says when the report is needed. Its number is permanent and never reused. Its title and text are rewritten freely, since the number is the key.

- A FACTS entry holds, after its number and a bold title that states the fact: what is established now, and under which conditions; what it means for the work, such as what it blocks or which row or decision it bears on; its evidence: the test that gates it, or its source, and whether it was observed, read in the code or inferred; the decision it builds, by number and subject; and the report section that holds the detail.
- A POSITIONS entry holds, after its number and a bold title: what the curator decided about the project, and why, in one or two sentences; where it applies; and what it requires of the work. It may point to a fact that it rests on, in the sentence that needs it. `P-48+` finds every fact that points to it.
- A POSITIONS entry states the curator's meaning in the record's register, and every fact in it is correct. It is the smallest text from which a fresh worker or coordinator, with the skills loaded, decides right. Workers and you decide by it where the curator is not asked, so a wrong premise in it spreads to each of those decisions.
- Give as an entry's reason the ground of its own case, such as the specification's text, the library's code or a measurement. Never give a rule that holds for every decision, such as the team's later word (P-26).
- POSITIONS holds only the curator's decisions. A choice that a worker made and landed without the curator's word is a fact about the tree. Its FACTS entry says that a worker chose it, and its review-queue item names that entry.
- An entry states the present, or what holds for all time. It holds no plan and no status: no state words such as "Built." or "Still to build:", no PLAN phase or item, no review-queue item, and no words that it waits for the curator's review. PLAN and the review queue name the entries that their items concern.
- If the tree does not yet do what a decision or the team's design asks, the missing part is a row of the gap ledger. The entry may name it as "row N", with a few words on what the row holds. In an entry, "row N" always names a row of the gap ledger.
- A pointer that stays in an entry carries a few words on what it holds, such as a ledger row's subject. A bare list of numbers goes to the history.
- A handle that only made sense in a past conversation, such as "answer 9", goes to the history.
- Quote the curator only where the exact words are the decision. Otherwise condense the words into the position, keeping the part of the rule that cuts. Check the condensed text against the words before you write it. The dictated words go to the history, with their time.
- A count that each landing changes has one entry with its current value, what it counts, the kinds with the largest share, and how to read a move. Other entries give its number. A count from one measurement says so.
- An entry holds one claim that can be kept up to date on its own, with its conditions, exceptions and evidence. Split an entry when its claims answer different questions and change apart. Before you split, look for an entry that already holds the claim, and move the text there. After a split, grep the record for the old number, and repoint each pointer that meant the claim that moved.
- If several entries together establish a conclusion that workers keep working out again, make it a sentence of the entry that owns its subject, with pointers to the entries it rests on. The pass updates it when one of them changes. Add a new entry only if no entry owns it. Leave a conclusion nobody has checked in its report, out of the entries.
- Keep an entry near 600 characters. This is a check, not a cap, and no reason to split: an entry may pass it if a question below keeps a sentence.
- Write halfway to ASD-STE100.

Ask of each sentence, and act on the answer:

1. Would the reader do otherwise without it? Keep it.
2. Would the reader misread another sentence without it? Keep it.
3. Does it tell how the fact came about: a date, a batch, a correction? Move it to the history.
4. Is it detail needed only while doing the work: a line number, a list of sites, a timing? Leave it in the report, and name the section.
5. Does another entry or a skill say it? Give that entry's number, or the skill's part.
6. Can a reader new to the project follow every word? Name the kind of each count.

In a consolidation of FACTS, judge each entry by six checks. Mark each one pass, fail, or unresolved where evidence is still needed, and quote the passage that fails:

- Scope: the title and the text agree on the path, the conditions and the limits, and claim no more than the evidence shows.
- Present meaning: a reader can tell the current property, or a measurement bounded to its day, without rebuilding a batch's work.
- Evidence: the cited support exists and holds the claim, and the entry states the kind of its evidence and its uncertainty.
- Comprehension: a reader can restate the fact and what it means. Subjects, referents and terms are plain.
- Ownership: the entry has one subject. No repair history or copied count hides it.
- Consistency: entries on the same subject agree, or state their different scopes or their conflict.

An entry that fails scope, evidence or consistency is not kept as it stands: reword it to what its support holds, or investigate where the support is unresolved. A fail of comprehension or ownership asks for a rewrite. Give no score: good prose does not make up for an unsupported claim. Then give the entry one disposition:

- keep: every check passes;
- reword: the meaning holds, but the wording or the stated scope fails;
- reorganize: move detail out, merge the entry into its owner, or split it;
- investigate: the support or the consistency is unresolved. Settle that narrow question before any new wording, and do not delete the fact meanwhile.

Before you write or check the first entries of a consolidation, read the five worked examples: `facts-extract.sh 'doc:explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/record-rule-draft.md#Worked examples'`, a large read.

## Reading and writing

- `git log -S'F-87' --oneline -- explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md` lists the commits that touched an entry.
- To read a history in depth, or a report's passage, send a Sonnet scout. The provenance lines tell it where to dig.
- `record.py`'s header gives its usage. `add`, `set`, `merge`, `remove` and `apply` write; each needs `--from PATH#HEADING` or `--note WHY`. The tool stamps the time and copies the earlier line to the history.
- Before every commit, run `record.py check --base <the commit before your edits>`. It shows that nothing was lost, and reports each entry over 600 characters.
- Commit the record file and its history together.
- Write a decision into POSITIONS in the next commit after the curator states it. A proposal of yours enters only at the curator's yes.
- The record is public and names models on purpose. Hold nothing back from it for that.

## The pass

Run the pass when a worker finishes, and before the next boot or batch reads FACTS. In a batch, the commit stage runs it, with this part quoted in its prompt. After a lone worker, you run it.

The pass owns each entry's final wording. A rung writes its findings as draft entries: the claim, its conditions, its evidence and what it means.

1. Write each new fact as an entry, or rewrite in place the entry that it changes. A rung writes its entries in a file `record.md` in its worktree, and the gather folds them in with `record.py apply`.
2. Give each change its provenance: the report section, the commit, and why.
3. Check each entry against its source, with bounded `grep`s:
   - The cited report section holds what the entry left out.
   - The entry keeps the source's scope: the path (walk or the compiled path), the call form (a dotted method call against a top-level call), the range of values and the conditions. Ask: does the entry let a reader conclude more than the evidence shows?
   - If a behaviour changed, grep FACTS for it, linked or not. Each entry that states it is updated, or says how it differs.
4. Cut any plan or status from each entry (above). If the cut text named a PLAN item or a review-queue item, check that the item names the entry.
5. Report each entry over 600 characters, with the question that keeps its extra sentence.

Run the same pass on POSITIONS at each landing, and when the curator replaces a decision.

## A consolidation

A consolidation runs the pass over whole sections. After a batch lands, the record-landing workflow consolidates its entries (`references/batch.md`, "The landing").

- In a consolidation, by hand or by the clarity or mining workflow, run a pilot of three or four entries first. Show their new texts to the curator as a page, each with its old text (`SKILL.md`, "Pages"). Run the rest on the curator's go. The pilot shows the curator the form: the length, the register, and what belongs in the history. The other checks, the pass's step 3, the tools' cold readers and the quiz, test only the meaning. The record-landing workflow takes no pilot, since it lands with no step of yours.
- Split each section into chunks of 20 to 32 entries.
- For each chunk, a Sonnet scout gathers each entry's report sections, its commits and the curator's dated words.
- An Opus writer reads this part, the chunk and the scout's file, and writes an apply file. It runs `apply` and `check --base` in its own worktree.
- You apply each file on `main`, run `check --base`, commit and push.
- Have Opus workers check each new entry by the pass's step 3. Run no Fable review of the entries.
- Have a fresh Opus worker answer a small quiz of decisions from the new entries, on the records at hand, without the curator. The decisions must stay as good, and the worker must follow the pointers when needed. If something critical is lost, find the middle ground entry by entry.

## The consolidation tools

Four Workflow scripts keep the record and the worker skill current and readable. Each one's README says how to run it and what to do with its output. Give a run only its arguments and the input files that its README names. Add no rules of your own over the tool's briefs, and change the briefs only where its README says to, such as their paths. If the briefs do not fit the job, propose their change to the curator. Put the open questions of the runs on the review queue.

Pick the tool by the job:

- To bring the record in line with a landing: the record-landing workflow (`references/batch.md`, "The landing"). Its README: `explorations/coordinator/tools/record-landing/README.md`.
- To find whether a POSITIONS entry comes from the curator's words or from an agent's summary or default: the mining workflow. Its writer changes only a sentence that is false, stale or not the curator's. Run it on the entries that it has not traced, before the clarity workflow rewrites them. Its README: `explorations/coordinator/positions-audit/README.md`.
- To make entries read on their own, with their meaning kept: the clarity workflow. For FACTS, it first judges every entry by the six checks of "What an entry is", and rewrites only those marked reword or reorganize. Its README: `explorations/coordinator/tools/record-clarity/README.md`.
- To correct the entries that a review's findings name: the clarity workflow, with `findings.md` in each chunk's folder, in the form that its README gives. An entry changes only where a finding names it, and grows only by what the correction needs.
- To keep `fortress-repo`'s revival part short enough to read whole: the orientation workflow. Its update mode runs after each landing. Run its consolidate mode when a cold read or the regression quiz shows that the part no longer reads whole, or when an update cannot keep it within the README's budget. Its README: `explorations/coordinator/tools/orientation/README.md`.

## INDEX and the gap ledger

- Give each new note under `explorations/` one line in INDEX, from its header comment's first sentence.
- Put a run's working files in an `evidence/` folder beside its results file: its briefs, chunks and checks, and the worker reports that the results draw on. Move them there with `git mv` once the results are judged. Only the results file gets an INDEX line. `check-index.sh` skips evidence folders. Do not add a folder's name to its list to let the folder pass.
- The gap ledger keeps its rows in topic sections. A row keeps its number for good. `explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py` is the only way to write it. Other views, such as `explorations/apl/lessons.md`, are derived from it.
- Split a rewrite of the ledger among small workers, each with a slice of rows that it can hold. Run a duplicate search first, as its own step.
- Ask the curator before you regroup the ledger's rows or derive its views again.

- P-173 **A numeral converts where it stands: where its place fixes a type, into that type at compile time from its exact value; where nothing fixes one, into the machine default, a `ZZ32`, or a `ZZ64` or `ZZ` when its value does not fit, and with a radix point an `RR64`.** A place fixes a type when its declared type has a coercion from the numeral type, as the eight number types have and a program's own type may (P-174), or is a numeral type; `Any`, `Object`, `Number`, an unbounded type parameter and no declared type take the default. So `x = 3` is a `ZZ32`, and `x SEQV z` is `true` for `z: ZZ32 = 3`; `bigN = 3000000000` is a `ZZ64` at its binding (row 946). The default applies to a numeral, a literal after the fold, never to an expression of a numeral type, and a `nat` parameter used as a value is a `ZZ32` (P-40). A type parameter that several numerals fix takes the narrowest default that holds every value, an `RR64` where any has a radix point, each numeral converting into it exactly; a float numeral whose conversions into `QQ` and `RR64` tie reads `RR64`. At a typed place the conversion is exact or rounds once (P-76, P-172), and a numeral outside the type's range is refused statically; walk converts from the exact value at the same places, place by place, before it runs the checker (P-12). An expression of numerals alone folds exactly before the checker into a signed constant, which defaults as an integer numeral, as a `QQ` for a quotient, or as an `RR64` with a radix point: so `x = 7/2` is a `QQ`, `1/2 = 0.5` is `true` through `QQ`'s `=` pair, and `-2147483648`, prefix minus on a numeral, folded, is a `ZZ32`. The library's `=` pairs over the numeral types stay, their conversion of a numeral folded. `gg(5, w)`, with `gg` declared at `(ZZ32, T)` and at `(Any, Any)`, runs the `ZZ32` declaration (P-49). Why: the design completes the Working Draft's, whose numerals have types of their own so that a library decides by coercions how they meet other types (P-174 gives that ground). It bends P-26 in two places, the numeral types' names and the places that fix no type, where the compiler's prelude, the team's later word, keeps the numeral's own type; the curator takes the bend by his right to finish the specification. He declined exact defaults, `ZZ` and `QQ` (the 2012 restart gives `NN` and `QQ`, `literals.tick:25`), since microGPT's untyped hyperparameters (`MicroGptFlat.fss:18`) would then be rationals and every untyped index would need `asZZ32`. The Draft's text that it contradicts, for Appendix I: numerals "not directly converted" and "polymorphic" (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/expressions/literals.tex:132-141`) at places that fix no type, and a `nat` parameter usable wherever an `NN32` variable is (`basic/trait-parameters.tex:84-86`); P-174 names the binary chapter's. What it keeps and changes in form: the judgement's section 3. POSITIONS.md:105
- P-174 **A numeral's own type is the Working Draft's, `NaturalNumeral` or, with a radix point, `RadixPointNumeral`, both below `Numeral`, and its value carries the Draft's four numbers as fields; a program's own number type receives a numeral through its coercion from that type, which the compiler calls once per class, when the class loads.** The four numbers are the digit count `n`, the digits after the radix point `m`, the radix `r`, and the digits read as one integer in that radix `v` (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/expressions/literals.tex:83-129`); they are fields of the value, not static parameters of the type, and the Draft's explicit-radix variants and `Literal[\v\]` fold into the radix field. The two types replace the implementations' `IntLiteral` (P-76) and `FloatLiteral` (P-172). A numeral type is written only as a parameter type, of a coercion or an operator, never as a variable's, field's or return type, so the library's `pi` and `e` (`Library/Constants.fsi:16-17`) are `RR64`. A program's type declares the coercion inside itself, such as `coerce(x: RadixPointNumeral)`, and reads the four numbers; the compiler emits the call with the numbers as constants, so a numeral at a program's type denotes one object per site, as a string literal does (P-171): in his words, "Coerce is just invocation of the numeric type constructor that gets the constants from the parser." A program's type with no coercion from the numeral type refuses a numeral. Inside a coercion's body two numeral values compare by their reduced value, so `2.5` and `2.50` are equal there, under `SEQV` too (P-168). Fields cannot make a size static, so the design contradicts the binary chapter's static word width from a numeral's digit count (`Specification-1.0-frozen/advanced-lib/binary.tex:1620-1621`, `:1659-1662`), for Appendix I, and drops its `opr ||` with a numeral. Why: the Draft gives numerals types of their own so that "library designers [can] decide how numerals should interact with other types of objects by defining coercion operations" (`literals.tex:141-145`), as an interval type should receive `3.1415926535897932384` unrounded (`:135-141`). The team built that coercion under its own names, with the exact value in the numeral ("ZZ32 now coerces IntLiteral as described in the spec", commit `128f313b5b`, 2009), but never the four numbers, and no team word calls the names temporary or final; the design keeps what they built, one type for each kind of numeral with its exact value at the coercion, and adds the Draft's names and numbers. The team's one word on a numeral's value at run time: "IntLiterals should always be transient objects with minimal lifetime" (`compiler/runtimeValues/FIntLiteral.java:21-23`, 2009). A coercion handed a double loses: a bfloat16 type then rounds `1.00390625000000000001` twice, to `0x3F80`, where one rounding gives `0x3F81`. P-173 weighs the bend of P-26. Detail: `reviews/literal-design-judgement-2026-11-08.md`, sections 1, 3 and 6; the prototype, `compile-ladder/plan-29/probes/literal-default.md`, sections 6 and 7.

The compiled checker checks sizes, and refuses a size beyond `NN32` or `ZZ32` (F-140, the bound on both paths). Wherever the array design, the compiled path's design for arrays (P-85), creates a JVM array, it checks the length there, at run time, and refuses one over 2^31-1. A size that inference leaves unknown is an error only when it reaches a type, a name or a value. So a declaration may declare a size that none of its types uses, and pass. A call that cannot fix a size of the declaration that it would choose is refused, also inside an overload set, instead of passing over that declaration. In the rule that no type extends two different instantiations of one generic trait, two instantiations differ when any static argument but an operator differs, so `Vec[\3\]` and `Vec[\4\]` are two; boolean arguments count too once the checker has boolean parameters. A size used as a number, as in the range `0#n`, converts to `ZZ32` where one is needed, as a numeral does. The 17 vector and matrix operators of the `FortressLibrary` api declare only the sizes that their types use, the change of `explorations/perf-probes/array-sites/e3-rebased.patch`. It finishes the team's own fix of 2008, which removed those sizes from the component only. The JVM length check waits for the array design; under walk such an array stops at its store's factory with walk's own error, which no catch sees (row 527). The checker still passes over a declaration whose unfixed size occurs in its own parameter type (row 400). The checker compares no boolean arguments (row 406).

No line of microGPT changes, and by reading its numerals keep their bits. POSITIONS.md:47
- P-49 **The compiled checker tries a call first by subtyping, without the expected type, and coerces its arguments only when that attempt is not kept.** The expected type is the type that the call's context requires. The checker's first attempt checks the call by subtyping alone, without the expected type. It keeps that attempt when its result converts to the expected type, by coercion if need be. If it does not keep that attempt, it tries coercion of the arguments, with the expected type. So a declaration that fits the arguments as they are is not passed over for one that coercion reaches. Code that its author called a stub, and code that works around a limit of the JVM or of the checker, serve only the implementation. The decision that they depart from stands. "Later" is the date of the team's work on the point at issue. The revival revises `Specification/` to follow a later decision. The one library follows it too, in place of the team's earlier code, such as the interpreter's library. Where two later decisions conflict, the goal decides (P-8). The implementers' later word also outweighs unfinished text. Why: the Working Draft's early text was a wish. The type group, the part of the team that built the type checker and the compiler, then worked to make the language run. So they learned what is feasible. They sought performance, and specialization was a must. Their later decisions include the exclusion rule, specialization and the number types of the compiler's prelude, siblings from 2009 to 2012 (P-43). The revival knows less than they did, so it does not second-guess them.

The split stops at a chunk that runs efficiently in sequence: in his words, "you need the right forking constants", as Steele's parallel trees end in sequential leaves and Clojure's persistent vectors take their branching factor from B-trees. It needs a group of forked arms to join every arm before it completes abruptly, which the compiled path does not do (`CodeGen.genParallelExprs` joins on the normal path only; `reviews/parallelism-foundations-2026-11-08.md`, section 7.1, its draft row N1). == explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md, ## Execution model; P-175 points to it

FACTS.md:13
- F-19 **By the specification, the iterations of a `for` loop, the elements of a tuple, and the arguments of a call or an operator may run in parallel, and a program must assume that they do.** A `for` loop is sequential only if every generator is, as `seq(g)` or `sequential(g)` makes it. An implementation may also run them one after another (`evaluation/parallelism.tex:88-90`), so a program cannot count on parallel runs either. For the elements of a tuple and the operands of an operator, each path starts a task only where it judges it worth it: walk by `TupleTask.worthSpawning`, which also governs a call's arguments, and the code generator by `ParallelismAnalyzer`. Compiled, a function call's arguments run in order (`CodeGen.evalArg`). A `for` loop over a range without `seq` runs by splitting the range into `do … also do … end` blocks. Under walk, every such block is a task, and walk's library splits down to single elements (`Library/RangeInternals.fss`). Compiled, the first block runs in place, and each other block forks only where `BaseTask.forkIfProfitable` judges it worth it, as tuple elements do; the compiler prelude's `parloop` splits down to `FORTRESS_LOOP_CHUNK` elements, 1 by default. `FORTRESS_THREADS` sizes the pool of worker threads (the `fortress-repo` skill, "Parallelism and mutable state"). By grep, no program under `explorations/`, the model programs and the probes, writes `spawn`, which starts an explicit thread, or an `also do` block, so their parallelism comes only from loops, tuples and arguments. The revival's tests under `ProjectFortress/` write both. Source: `Specification/basic/expressions/for.tex:28-32`, `tuple-expr.tex:23-24`, `operator-app.tex:58-59`, `evaluation/parallelism.tex:50-80`.

## The row template

A row is one line of eight cells, `| # | claim | status | class | spec citation | reproducer | found by | notes / workaround |`, at most 1,200 characters, in the table of its topic section, in number order. A pipe inside a cell is written `\|`. (POSITIONS, "The gap ledger's form"; the proposal behind it is `explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/gap-ledger-archaeology.md`, section 4.)

- **#**: the row's number, the next free one when it is added; never reused, renumbered or given to another row. 148 is vacant.
- **claim**: at most 300 characters, whose first 150 name the defect or the capability: what fails or what holds, and where.
- **status**: exactly one word of seven, with no second status and nothing in brackets:
  - `POSITIVE-VERIFIED`: it works; it ran and its output is recorded.
  - `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`: the specification settles it and the reproducer confirms it. A row with one half fixed stays `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`, and its notes say which half is fixed.
  - `NEGATIVE-BOUNDED`: the failure reproduces; the mechanisms tried are named and are not exhaustive.
  - `CONTESTED`: unsettled; the notes say why.
  - `RETIRED`: a source's claim falsified here, kept so that it is not derived again.
  - `FIXED`: closed by a landed commit (`ledger.py close`): the claim's first sentence, the test as reproducer, notes `fixed HASH; full text: history, row N`.
  - `DUPLICATE`: a pointer (`ledger.py duplicate`), notes `duplicate of row M; full text: history, row N`.
- **class**: `kind (area)`; `—` only for `POSITIVE-VERIFIED` and `RETIRED`. The kind is one of `implementation gap`, `library gap vs spec`, `library bug`, `design limit`, `deliberate`, `typesetter`, `packaging`; the area one of `parser`, `walk`, `checker`, `codegen`, `runtime`, `library`, `prelude`, `specification`, `tests`, `tools`.
- **spec citation**: the `.tex` file and the section heading in quotes, as `basic/operators/juxtameaning.tex`, "Juxtaposition"; a line number only against `Specification-1.0-frozen/`; `silent` where the specification does not say.
- **reproducer**: one test (its name, or its path under the test folders; an `XXX` test while it is an expected failure) or one probe path from the repository root, at most 200 characters; `none` when nothing in the tree reproduces it, with the command and its output, or the probe's old path, in the notes.
- **found by**: the stream that found it (`climb batch 8 rung I`, `run-c3`, `apl rung 2`), at most 60 characters; no date and no role.
- **notes / workaround**: at most 700 characters: `siblings: N, M` first if there are any; the mechanism, with file:line and the commit it was true at; the workaround; for a closed row, `fixed HASH`.

A path under `explorations/` that is no longer in the tree is read from history: `git show $(git log -1 --diff-filter=D --format=%h -- PATH)^:PATH`.

# Judgement: the numeral design of 2026-11-08

## 1. Coherence

The design is one rule: a numeral converts where it stands, into the declared type, else into the machine default. Six cases get two answers or none; each has a repair.

- Undefined: what "fixes a type". Point 1 lists `Any`; the fork review adds `Object`, `Number` and an unbounded `T` (§1.1); the prototype defaulted at all (probe §1, step 2). Repair: a place fixes a type when its declared type declares a coercion from the numeral type (the eight number types; a program's type by point 4) or is a numeral type; every other type, and no type, takes the default. Then `f(3)` at `Number` is a `ZZ32`, and a tuple at `Any` defaults element by element.
- Two answers: "by its value" where the value is unknown. Row 946 shows it: a variable of numeral type reads `ZZ32` whatever its value. Inside `coerce(x: RadixPointNumeral)`, `t = x` is such an expression; so is a `nat` used as a value, whose value a template does not know (probe §8). Repair: the default applies to a numeral, a literal after the fold, never to an expression of numeral type; a `nat` used as a value has the type the Draft gives, `NN32` (`trait-parameters.tex:84-86`), or `ZZ32` (P-40), chosen once.
- Two answers: the fold against the fields. Point 4 reads the written numeral's four numbers; point 5 folds `7/2`, `-3` and `0.1 + 0.2` into "one numeral", which has no written form: the prototype made `1/3` a radix-3 numeral (probe §1, step 3), and a negative result has no `nat v`. Repair: the fold yields a constant with a sign, as the Draft's `IntegerConstant[\false, 3+5\]` has one (`constant.tex:49-52`): an integer constant defaults as an integer numeral, a quotient to `QQ`, one with a radix point to `RR64`; a program's coercion sees the four numbers of a written numeral only.
- Two answers: a static argument that several numerals fix. `<|3000000000, 0.5|>` is a `List[\RR64\]` if each numeral converts exactly into one instantiation, refused if each defaults first (`ZZ64` into `RR64` is written, P-74); an `if` join likewise. Repair: the narrowest default holding every value, `RR64` where any has a radix point, each converting into it exactly: the tie rule's form (`inference.tex:313-317`).
- Two answers: a program's type with no coercion from the numeral type. The prototype chained default and own coercion (probe §10, decision 3); the Draft says coercion does not chain (`conversions-coercions.tex:407-408`). Repair: refuse, or name the chain as the one exception.
- Undefined: "once per class, at load" as a semantics. For a reference object two evaluations of `c: CC64 = 3` become one object, which `SEQV` sees (`objects.tex:51-53`), and a raising coercion fails at load. Repair: a numeral at a program's type denotes one object, as a string literal does (P-171), or hoist value types only.
- One answer, for the record: `-3` is `-` on a numeral (`lexical-structure.tex:1053-1080`); folded, `-2147483648` fits `ZZ32` and `u: NN32 = -3` is refused. `x = 3` then `x` at `ZZ64` converts (P-74), at `NN32` is refused (fork §6.1), point 1's rule. `pi: RadixPointNumeral` (`Constants.fsi:16-17`) is refused by the fifth default and becomes `RR64`. Two numeral values inside a body: by P-168 value objects compare field by field, so `2.5` and `2.50` differ there, as the Draft's types differ; elsewhere both default and are `SEQV`.

## 2. Against the record

- Revised: P-76 (the name; "walk's half" once walk has static types, which the default makes walk's rule today; `IntLiteral`'s arithmetic, which the fold retires). P-172: the name; "Where nothing fixes a type ... the numeral stays an exact `FloatLiteral`: `Cell(0.5)` is a `Cell[\FloatLiteral\]`"; "prints a bare numeral as written, as the team's `tests/NumberPrintTest.fss:16` asserts", a team test that now breaks; its two open items close.
- Facts: F-79, F-57 (the checker's two types), F-169 (the text's `IntLiteral`), F-73 (the tie reading becomes the rule, floats included), F-74 (walk's numeral by value, a gap made the rule), F-118, F-262. P-169: the 24 numeral glue bindings and their carrier fall away (probe §4.5).
- Bent: P-26. The prelude keeps the numeral's type at every untyped place (fork §3.3), code "built alike for all its types"; the Draft's types are unfinished text (F-169), the names the implementers' later word. No team word calls them temporary (scout §10). The one team word for point 4: "IntLiterals should always be transient objects with minimal lifetime" (`compiler/runtimeValues/FIntLiteral.java:21-23`, 2009). The entry should own the weighing as the curator's.
- Unchanged: P-168, P-171, P-165 (a name only), P-49, P-46, P-40, P-74.

## 3. Against the Draft

- Kept as written: `literals.tex:25-26` (literals are values); `:141-148` (library designers decide by coercions; coercions to integers and rationals); `:163` (`3.125` is `3125/1000`, at a `QQ` place); `:170-173` (one rounding); `variables.tex:75` (the variable's type is the initializer's).

## Summary

Verdict: coherent with the changes named below; as stated, four cases get two answers and two are undefined.

The design's one rule, convert where the numeral stands, into the declared type or else the machine default, answers the ordinary cases alike on both paths. The changes it needs: define "fixes a type" as a declared type with a coercion from the numeral type; apply the default to numerals only, never to an expression of numeral type, and give a `nat` used as a value one type; let the fold yield a signed constant whose quotient defaults to `QQ`, so that `x = 7/2` stays a `QQ` and `-2147483648` fits `ZZ32`; instantiate a type parameter that several numerals fix at the narrowest default holding them all; say whether a program's type without a coercion from the numeral type is refused or chained; and state "once per class" as a rule about objects, or hoist value types only.

It revises P-76 and P-172 (the names, the exact-where-unfixed clause, printing as written), six facts, and bends P-26, which the entry should own as the curator's weighing: the team's one word for it is that literals "should always be transient objects". Against the Draft it keeps literals as values, coercions as the library's device and one rounding; makes the four numbers fields; and contradicts "not directly converted" at untyped places and the binary chapter's static width, which fields cannot feed.

The sub-choices follow from the points, except `x = 7/2`, which needs the fold repaired, and the fold itself, which is free and which the Draft favours. Forty-two programs pin the design; the prototype measured most compiled ones; microGPT changes no line and no bit, by reading only. Ten questions stay open.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""The gap ledger's tool: it owns the ledger's format, reads its rows, and is
the only way to write them.

The ledger, explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md, is sorted into topic sections,
each a "## TITLE" heading over one table of rows. A row is one line of eight
cells, and keeps its number wherever it sits:

  | # | claim | status | class | spec citation | reproducer | found by | notes / workaround |

The template (POSITIONS.md, "The gap ledger's form"; the proposal behind it is
explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/gap-ledger-archaeology.md, 4.1):
  status       exactly one of POSITIVE-VERIFIED, NEGATIVE-VERIFIED,
               NEGATIVE-BOUNDED, CONTESTED, RETIRED, FIXED, DUPLICATE
  class        `kind (area)`, kind one of the legend's seven, area one of ten;
               `—` only for POSITIVE-VERIFIED and RETIRED
  spec         the .tex file and the section heading in quotes; a line number
               only against Specification-1.0-frozen/; `silent` where the
               specification does not say
  reproducer   one test (a name under the test folders, or a path) or probe
               path from the repository root, or `none`
  limits       row 1,200 characters, claim 300, reproducer 200, found by 60,
               notes 700
  a pipe inside a cell is written \\|

Cells are split only at a pipe that is not escaped as \\|. A row whose cells
hold bare pipes (the ledger had six) does not split into its table's width that
way; it is read by its split at pipes followed by a space or the line's end, as
facts-extract.py has always read it, and check reports it under `pipe`.

Every write takes a lock (flock on .ledger.lock beside the ledger), checks the
template on the line it writes, and puts the full earlier line of a row it
changes, unchanged, in the history file beside the ledger
(fortress-gap-ledger-history.md), under "### Row N" and a line saying what
became of it. A failed check prints the rules the row breaks and exits 1.
add, rewrite, close and duplicate check the whole line they write; note checks
only what it changes (the notes cell and the row's length), so that a row
failing the template elsewhere still takes a note. A row at its length limit
takes no note: rewrite cuts it back (the rework's decision D4, "each is cut
when next edited", process-engineering/gap-ledger-archaeology.md).

usage: ledger.py COMMAND [ARGS] [--root DIR] [--ledger FILE] [--history FILE]

  heads                      one tab-separated line per row: number, status,
                             class, the claim's first 150 characters, and the
                             paths the row cites in backticks
  sections                   each section that holds a row table: its row
                             count and title, tab-separated
  section TITLE              the heads of that section's rows
  show N [--short]           row N under its section and table header; with
                             --short, its status, class, claim and the notes'
                             first 300 characters
  find WORDS [--open] [--cites FILE[:LINE]] [--all]
                             one line per row that holds every word (whole
                             words, or a word's start with a trailing *):
                             number, status, class, the claim's start; --open
                             leaves out FIXED, DUPLICATE and RETIRED; --cites
                             keeps the rows citing FILE (at LINE) and prints
                             the lines they cite; at most 10 rows unless --all
  count                      the rows by status, kind and area; nothing stored
  add FILE --section TITLE   FILE holds one row line, its # cell `?` (or the
                             seven cells after it); numbers it max + 1 and
                             inserts it in that section's table in number
                             order
  note N TEXT [--check]      adds TEXT to row N's notes, before the row's own
                             "full text: history, row N" marker where it has
                             one, else at their end (notes of `none` are
                             replaced); checks the notes cell and the row's
                             length only, so a failure in another cell does
                             not block it; a row keeps its own cells. With
                             --check it writes nothing: it prints whether
                             TEXT fits, and the characters that the notes
                             (700) and the row (1,200) would have left with
                             it and have left now; exit 0 if it fits, 1 if
                             not, so a note is sized before it is written
  rewrite N FILE             FILE holds row N's whole new line (its # cell N
                             or ?, or the seven cells after it); checks it
                             against the template and writes it in the row's
                             place, its earlier line in the history
                             ("rewritten"): the route that corrects a claim,

                             The files are the tree's (FACTS, POSITIONS, the

Text given on the command line (TEXT, C) has its bare pipes escaped.

# Setting up, building, the caches, and what to rebuild

**tree**
: Checkout of the repository: the main checkout or a worktree. In a command, `<tree>` is the tree that you work in: the one that your brief names, else the one that your session starts in.

**library order**
: Five compiles that build the compiled path's library into the caches.

**DSL grammar**
: `grammar` declaration in an api, which adds syntax for a domain-specific language.

**parser directory**
: New `fortress<random>rats` folder of 5.8 MB, in which a program that imports a DSL grammar gets a Rats! parser generated when it runs. The run makes it in its JVM's temporary directory and never deletes it.

## Setting up each call

Start every Bash call with these lines. They put you at the tree's root, where this skill's commands start unless they `cd`:

    cd <tree> && mkdir -p tmp
    export JAVA_HOME=/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64 PATH=/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64/bin:$PATH
    export FORTRESS_HOME=$PWD FORTRESS_THREADS=1 TMPDIR=$PWD/tmp JAVA_FLAGS="-Xmx4g -Xss64m -Djava.io.tmpdir=$PWD/tmp"
    unset JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS

- If `/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64` or `ant` is missing, run `apt-get update -qq && apt-get install -y openjdk-25-jdk-headless ant` first.
- `bin/fortress` takes `FORTRESS_HOME` from the shell whenever it is set. If it names another tree, you run that tree's code. Check it with `echo $FORTRESS_HOME`.
- `JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS` is unset, because the proxy's trust-store flags in it break ant's JVM forks.

The lines give the settings of `explorations/experiment/env.sh`, with two differences:

- The JVM's temporary directory is your tree's `tmp/`, which is gitignored.
- They leave out env.sh's removal of old parser directories in `/tmp`, because your runs put theirs in your tree's `tmp/` (below).

If your brief tells you to run `source env.sh` and then to point `TMPDIR` and `JAVA_FLAGS` at `tmp/`, use the lines above. They do the same.

The library and microGPT import no DSL grammar, and of the gated tests only `ProjectFortress/syntax_abstraction_tests/ForUse.fss` does. The ungated tests beside it import one, and so do the APL experiments under `explorations/apl/`.

With the lines above, your runs that import a DSL grammar put their parser directories in `<tree>/tmp/`. Hundreds of them once filled the disk allowance. So:

- When no run of yours is live, remove yours: `rm -rf <tree>/tmp/fortress*rats`.
- Before a long run, check `df -h /`. How to read it: the `cloud-container` skill.

## Two layers of code

The repository holds two layers of code. Different tools build them, at different times, so "compile" means a different thing in each layer.

The implementation is the parser, walk, the compiled checker, the code generator and the runtime. It is the Java and Scala under `ProjectFortress/src/`, with the parser grammars (`parser/*.rats`) and the syntax tree generated from `ProjectFortress/astgen/Fortress.ast`. `ant compileAll` builds it into `ProjectFortress/build/` ("Building", below). `ant compile` is another name for it.

The Fortress code is the library, the tests and the programs: the `.fss` and `.fsi` files. The `fortress` commands run the phases on it and keep the results in the caches:

- Walk runs the phases on each component that a run needs. It needs no `fortress compile`.
- `fortress compile` writes a component's jar. It is for the compiled path's components only: the compiler's library, compiled tests and compiled programs.
- `fortress run` compiles no Fortress source.
- A command reuses an entry if no source that the entry depends on is newer than the entry: its own source, and the `.fsi` files of the apis that it imports, at any depth.

An edit makes stale what was built from it:

- Java or Scala: the classes in `ProjectFortress/build/`. Run `ant compileAll`. The cache entries that the edited code wrote are stale too, and no entry notices it: an entry is compared with its sources, never with the implementation. For example, after a change to a native helper's signature, its old wrapper stays in `nativewrapper_cache/`, and the run links the old signature. For this reason, the build deletes the caches when the implementation changes ("Building").
- A parser grammar: the generated parser, and every entry that it parsed. Run `ant compileAll`.
- A `.fss` or `.fsi` file of the library: the entries of that component, and after an `.fsi` edit, the entries of every component that imports the api. Walk analyses them again by itself. A component of the compiler's library needs a compile, or the library order ("After an edit of the library").
- A test or a program: its own entries. Walk and the harness analyse a walk test again by themselves. Compile a compiled test or program again, or let the harness do it.

- Before you add or fix a language feature, print its row of the feature table. WORD names the feature, such as `spawn`, `coercion` or `typecase`. A row is about 1 KB. It names the feature's section of the specification, its parser rule, checker class, walk site, code-generator site, prelude declaration and ledger rows.

      explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'map:spec-to-implementation.md#Feature by feature@WORD'

- If your edit is in one phase, and you need what runs before and after it on each path, print that phase's section. Name the section by its number and the first word of its title. A section is 1 to 3 KB. B.1 is the phase list, B.4 disambiguation, B.5 desugaring, B.6 type checking, B.7 overloading, B.10 the caches, B.11 the runtime and B.12 the natives.

      explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'map:modules-and-phases.md#B.5 Desugaring'

- Before you change the text of a diagnostic, grep the `.test` files for it. A `.test` file can pin a whole diagnostic with `compile_err_equals`, its `file:line:column` included. `grep -l 'TEXT' ProjectFortress/*tests/*.test`, with words of the diagnostic as TEXT, lists the files that pin it. Update each of those in the same commit. A line that you add to or remove from a compiler test program moves the pinned spans below it.

## Testing an edit here

- For a quick loop on an edit of the checker or the code generator, compile the edited class into a scratch directory, and run the compiler with that directory first on its class path. Give each run a fresh copy of the caches, because nothing checks the caches against the compiler that wrote them, and a compile of an unchanged program with a jar writes nothing:

      Q=$PWD/tmp/quick ; export FORTRESS_CACHES=$Q/caches ; CP=$(bin/fortress_classpath | tail -1)
      mkdir -p $Q/classes && javac -nowarn -cp "$CP" -d $Q/classes ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/<path>/X.java
      rm -rf $Q/caches && cp -a default_repository/caches $Q/caches
      java $JAVA_FLAGS -Dfile.encoding=UTF-8 -Dfortress.caches=$Q/caches -cp "$Q/classes:$CP" com.sun.fortress.Shell compile P.fss
      bin/fortress run P

  For a Scala file, compile it with `java -cp "$CP" scala.tools.nsc.Main -classpath "$CP" -d $Q/classes -encoding UTF-8 X.scala`. Then put the edit into the tree and build it for real.
- If your change is near transactions, top-level mutable state or the class loader's first load, do the four-thread atomic runs (`gate.md`).

## The checker's time

This section is for a change of the checker: its Scala under `scala_src/`, or `ProjectFortress/astgen/Fortress.ast` and the generators under `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/astgen/`, from which the build generates the checker's syntax tree and `Walker`.

The count stage takes `<out-file> <scratch>` and about 80 to 180 seconds, more under load. It can run past the Bash tool's 120-second limit, so run it in the background (`session.md`). It writes a table to the out-file: the errors of each api, the total, the number of places with errors, and the first crash. It keeps the checker's whole output in `<scratch>/run.txt`, and its caches in `<scratch>`, so a run from the base build leaves the base build as it was.

The checker checks every api first, and the component only if no api has an error. In each api or component, it stops at the first of its stages that finds errors. The stages run in this order (`compiler/StaticChecker.java`, `checkCompilationUnit`):

1. The type hierarchy and the type check.
2. The overloading check, which also compares the overloads' return types.
3. In the component only, the export check (`library.md`, "Designing a change").

So the count misses the errors of the later stages, and a fix of an early error can raise it.

content.content:
## The `fortress` commands

`Shell.java` dispatches `bin/fortress <command>`.

- To see what an early phase makes of a program, stop after that phase: `parse` (a syntax check), `disambiguate`, `grammar`, `desugar` or `typecheck`.
- `unparse` prints the syntax tree back as Fortress source. Use it to see what a desugaring made.
- `link` links a compiled component (the `link` step of a compiled `.test` file). `api` writes a component's api. `test` runs a program's `test` declarations under walk.
- The command chooses the library. Walk and `test` call `Shell.useInterpreterLibraries()`. Every other command calls `useCompilerLibraries()`. Each call points `WellKnownNames` and `Types` to its prelude, and sets the desugaring switches.

## Running

    cd ProjectFortress
    # after an ant compileAll that started the caches again: the library order (build-and-caches.md)
    ../bin/fortress compile <path>/P.fss
    ../bin/fortress run P [args]

A small program compiles in about 5 s and runs in about 1 s.

- A crash of the checker prints one line and hides the Java stack. To see the stack, put `-debug stacktrace` before the file: `../bin/fortress compile -debug stacktrace <path>/P.fss`.
- A failed compile of a program leaves a 0-byte jar in `bytecode_cache/`. A run of the program then prints "Could not load P" and "Resource not found". Read the compile's error instead.

8:- **Where the base matters.** The base 157323e51 lacks rung A's slot API (`TXReadSlot`, `TXWriteSlot`, `FortressArrayStore`). This matters only for the store's init race (§7, row N7), which ran on

## 8. What I could not build or measure

- **No compiled run on the one library.** Every one-library answer in this report is the checker's static type (section 4.4); the run-time answers of section 5 are by reading. The switch-over is not done.
- **Joins** (`if`, `case` of numerals at an untyped binding) and **tuples** of numerals as one argument at `Any` are not built: the whole expression is coerced, so the branches still make literal values.
- **`QQ`'s fold**: a numeral at a `QQ` place still calls the coercion with a literal value; the prelude has no `QQ` to test against.
- **`nat` parameters used as values** are expressions of type `IntLiteral` (the code generator builds them as `IntLiteral` constants, the comment at `CodeGen.java:6339` at the base); the default coerces them at run time, so a literal value still exists there. Section 5's string-juxtaposition sites are of this kind.
- **The 12 other components'** default sites: `WorldFlip` given the 14 files in one run printed only `FortressLibrary`'s (81 lines), and the distance stage printed none of the trace (its run captures standard error, but no `LITERAL-DEFAULT` line appeared); I traced `String` alone and did not run the other 12 one by one.
- **The demos** (`tests-running.md`, "Outside the gate") were not run: the library change edits walk's library, and walk's float ties already fail 71 tests, so the driver's verdict would carry no news about B.
- **The specification's text** for B (review §5.3) is not written: this is a prototype.
- **Timing beyond the smoke test**: no profile, no second pass.

## 9. Defects found

- **The `=` pairs over `IntLiteral` dropped breaks the one library's comparisons with a numeral under A, and `NN32`'s, `NN64`'s and `RR32`'s against an integer numeral under B**, by reading (section 5). A defect of the brief's sub-choice, not of the tree; under B it needs either the pairs kept and folded, or `=` pairs from `ZZ32` into the unsigned types, which P-74 forbids as implicit coercions. Recorded here only: no gated test can show it before the switch-over (`tests-writing.md`, "How a defect is recorded", item 3; its row is for the curator's decision, below).

content.content:
## Decisions

1. **Compiled probes in a worktree at main, repeated on the base for attribution.** Every new compiled defect reproduces on 157323e5. So N1–N6 and N8 are the team's code; N7 is batch 28's own line. The alternative, the base alone, would not have reached the slot API. No decision of the curator covers this; I followed the brief.
2. **The store's init race tested at Java level,** with `ArrayStoreJUTest`'s protocol, because no compiled program reaches the one library's arrays before the switch-over. The alternative, waiting for the switch-over, leaves A.skeptic.3 unmeasured.
3. **No rows for the four reading-only findings (§7.3).** None is reproduced as a program-level defect. The alternative was rows marked NEGATIVE-BOUNDED.
4. **A rewrite of row 933 rather than a sibling row.** It is one mechanism with two symptoms. The alternative is a new row, siblings 933.
5. **Timing only on the compiled path** (P-29), at one and four threads, alone on the machine.

## Questions for the curator (decisions not taken)

- **D1. Arrays of unboxed numbers and `atomic` (P-84, P-169).** P-169's own reason is that "a compiled atomic write into any array needs that keying". Today the slot API keys only `Object[]`, the `double[]` store "takes no part in a transaction", and N8 shows what an untracked store does under `atomic`. The options:
  - (a) Unboxed stores stay outside transactions. This is recorded as a departure in Appendix I. It contradicts P-169's reason.
  - (b) A primitive slot API, `TXReadDouble` and `TXWriteDouble`, validated by raw bits (NaN and -0.0 make `!=` wrong), plus a per-element check of about 1–2 ns (row 641's rate).
  - (c) The library checks once per bulk operation, `fill`, `map` or `mul`, and picks a transactional or a plain loop.

  There is no default on record. microGPT needs none of (b) or (c) for correctness.
- **D2. Strong atomicity on the compiled path** (N2; `atomic.tex:100-106`). The options:
  - (a) Keep weak atomicity for programs outside the discipline, recorded in Appendix I.
  - (b) Plain writes of mutable variables take the sequence lock: a compare-and-set pair per plain write.
  - (c) The specification's shared and local objects (`shared-local.tex`), so that only shared objects pay.

  Disciplined programs, microGPT among them, are unaffected by (a).
- **D3. Parallel reductions on the compiled path** (N5). The options:
  - (a) The code generator forks call arguments by `ParallelismAnalyzer`, as it does tuples.
  - (b) The one library's `generate` binds its halves as a tuple.
  - (c) Leave them sequential until PLAN's "compiled parallelism" (inventory B1 steps 20 and 21).

  This bears on PLAN's order.

## For FACTS

1. **Walk's STM descends from DSTM2 and is strongly atomic.** It has visible readers, eager conflict detection, and a manager that always aborts the other transaction, chosen for work stealing.
   - For the work: walk is the reference for the specification's semantics of `atomic`.
   - Check: `git show 9aed945d8:ProjectFortress/src/dstm2/manager/GreedyManager.java` against `GreedyManager.java:22-49`; `WStrongAtomicity` printed 0 of 300.
   - Detail: §§1.2, 2.
2. **The compiled STM is in NOrec's form: one global sequence lock, buffered writes, value validation, closed nesting.** Flood wrote it in April–May 2012.
   - For the work: its commits do not scale; a contended counter is slower at four threads than at one.
   - Numbers: about 210 ns per uncontended block against 15 ns plain; 351–602 against 225–335 ns per contended update.
   - Check: `runcost.sh` (§3.3). Detail: §§1.4, 2, 3.3.
3. **Compiled reductions run their bodies one at a time,** because call arguments are evaluated in order. This follows from F-19's evalArg sentence, which does not draw it.
   - Check: `CReductionPar` printed "at most 1 at once". Row N5.
4. **Neither microGPT program opens a transaction; their gather is reductions and products.**
   - Check: `grep -n -E '\batomic\b|\bspawn\b|\balso\b' explorations/run-c4/src/*.fss explorations/apl/mg/*.fss`, no match.
   - Detail: §6.
5. **F-185's commented-out multi-threaded half passes when restored with `invokeAll`:** 2048 of 2048, five runs. The comment-out came from an API change.
   - Check: `java/probe/ReadSetThreads.java`. Detail: §2.

content.content:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""The record's tool: it owns the form of FACTS.md and POSITIONS.md and of
their two history files, and is the only way to write them.

An entry is one line under a permanent number, `- F-87 **Title.** Text.` in
explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md and `- P-48 **Title.** Text.` in
POSITIONS.md. A number is never reused or changed: a new entry takes the
highest number its file has ever used, plus one. An entry stands under the
nearest `## ` or `### ` heading above it, its section. Its title is its bold
opening, or where it has none, its opening words up to the first colon,
semicolon or full stop.

A pointer is another entry's number in the sentence that needs it, alone
(`It builds P-48.`) or with the first words of the target's title in quotes
(`It builds P-48, "A type parameter the arguments do not fix ..."`, or
`P-48 ("...")`). Quoted words must open the target's current title (`...` or
`…` marks words left out); when an entry is retitled, the tool rewrites them
in every entry that points to it, in the same call.

The history (FACTS-history.md, POSITIONS-history.md beside the record) holds,
under `### F-87`, one block per change, oldest first: one provenance line (the
UTC time from the clock, the kind of change, `from` each report section,
`commit`, `by`, then the note after a colon), and the line as it stood before
the change. The tool derives the kind: `added`, `rewritten`, `moved to "S"`,
`merged into F-n`, `F-n merged in`, `removed`, `noted`; the numbering wrote one
`numbered` block per entry. A retitle that refreshed other entries' pointer
words, or a merge that moved their pointers, says so in one more line of the
block (`pointer words refreshed in: F-12, P-48`).

A `noted` block, which `note` writes, leaves the entry as it is. It adds what
the entry's history lacks, such as the curator's messages behind a text kept
word for word, with their times, or a correction of an earlier block. It holds
no earlier line, and its note says what it adds, so it needs one. A gone entry
takes none: its last block stays `merged into` or `removed`. A noted block
that corrects an earlier block names it by its time, in the field after the
kind: `correcting the block of 2026-10-13 19:07Z`, or, where blocks of the
entry share that minute, `correcting the 2nd block of 2026-10-14 04:41Z`,
counted oldest first. The block corrected is never edited.

Every write takes a lock (flock on .record.lock beside the record), checks the
state it would leave, appends the history blocks first and then replaces each
record file in one step. A write is refused only for what would break the
store: a bad number, a pointer that does not resolve or whose words do not
open its target's title, a line break in an entry, no provenance (neither
`--from` nor `--note`; for a noted block, no `--note`), a correction that
names no block or more than one, two blocks for one entry in one call.
Never for size. The tool does not commit: commit the record file and its
history together.

usage: record.py COMMAND [ARGS] [PROVENANCE] [--root DIR]

  PROVENANCE: --from PATH#HEADING (repeatable; PATH from the repository root
  or from explorations/, HEADING held by exactly one heading of it, as doc:
  resolves one), --commit HASH (in HEAD's history), --by WHO, --note WHY.
  Each write needs --from or --note.

  add F|P --section TITLE FILE   a new entry from FILE's one line, numbered
      record.py add F --section 'Landed semantics' new.md --from 'compile-ladder/rung-x/REPORT.md#The fix' --by coordinator
  set N [FILE] [--section TITLE] entry N rewritten from FILE's line, or moved
      record.py set F-87 f87.md --from 'compile-ladder/rung-x/REPORT.md#The question' --note 'cut to the form'
  merge N --into M [FILE]        N removed, M rewritten from FILE (or kept),
                                 every pointer to N made a pointer to M
      record.py merge F-90 --into F-87 f87.md --note 'one fact, two entries'
  remove N                       N removed; refused while a pointer to it remains
      record.py remove P-131 --note 'evicted to the coordinator skill, references/briefing.md'
  note N [--correcting TIME]     a noted block in N's history, N unchanged; needs
                                 --note; refused when the history holds it already.

content.content:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Checks explorations/coordinator/INDEX.md against the tree: which standalone
# notes are missing a line, which lines name a file that is gone, which lines
# fall outside the set the index is meant to cover, and which paths named in a
# line's prose no longer resolve. Read-only. Exit 1 if the first two are
# non-empty.
#
# The note set is every *.md under explorations/ except run/experiment trees
# (which document themselves in their own README) and evidence directories.
# Edit the two lists below when the shape of the tree changes.

set -uo pipefail

root=$(cd -- "$(dirname -- "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")/../.." && pwd)
index="$root/explorations/coordinator/INDEX.md"
[ -f "$index" ] || { echo "no INDEX.md at $index" >&2; exit 2; }

# Run/experiment trees: a directory holding one run's sources and evidence.
run_roots='apl|astra|blinded-fable|compile-ladder|run-b|run-b2|run-c|run-c3|run-c4|fortify|ci|experiment'
# Generic evidence directory names, at any depth.
evidence_dirs='probes|checks|goldens|figures|evidence|measurements|raw|src|tools|gate|cold-cache|reference|archive|build|article|worker|notes|recovered-reports|_prior|__pycache__|existing-tests|failed|png|regen|tic-regen|tour|pairs|combos'

notes=$(cd "$root" && find explorations -name '*.md' \
  | grep -vE "(^|/)[A-Za-z0-9_.-]+-(probes|pairs)/" \
  | grep -vE "(^|/)($evidence_dirs)/" \
  | grep -vE "^explorations/($run_roots)/" \
  | grep -v '^explorations/coordinator/INDEX.md$' \
  | sort)

# Entry keys: the backticked path at the start of an index bullet.
keys=$(grep -oP '^- `\K[^`]+' "$index" | sort -u)
# Entry keys that are notes (drop the .js/.sh entries from the comparison set).
key_notes=$(printf '%s\n' "$keys" | grep '\.md$' | sort -u)

missing=$(comm -23 <(printf '%s\n' "$notes") <(printf '%s\n' "$key_notes"))
stale=$(printf '%s\n' "$keys" | while read -r p; do
  [ -n "$p" ] && [ ! -e "$root/$p" ] && echo "$p"
done)
outside=$(comm -13 <(printf '%s\n' "$notes") <(printf '%s\n' "$key_notes"))

# Evidence: did the team treat IntLiteral/FloatLiteral as the design or a stopgap?

Scout: words only, no judgement. Repository /home/user/fortress. Each item: command, source, author, date, words.

## 0. Caveat on this repository's history (affects every blame)

The repository holds the team's history in disconnected pieces. There are 147 root commits dated before 2013 (`git log --max-parents=0`), each a full tree. The 2007 to 2009-10 chain (to `3e0306166d`) and 2011-03 onward are separate pieces; `git blame` at HEAD attributes every unchanged team line to root `5a68404fdf` (David Chase, 2012-07-19, "Added odd random longs to MagicNumbers"), which is a snapshot, not the author. Full message of `fca589bbb0` (jmaessen, 2008-07-15):
```
IntLiteral is now a subtype of ZZ32 (and thus of every other numeric
type).  But there are a number of caveats:
* ZZ32 is now a trait, with subtypes Int and IntLiteral.  In practice
all the ZZ32 math you do will end up yielding results of type Int.
This means that when you stuff the results into a polymorphically-typed
container (such as Maybe or List) the type variable will invariably be
dynamically instantiated with Int, rather than ZZ32 as you'd expect.
Most of the changes in this checkin address this in the regression
tests.
* In order to obtain the expected behavior with large constants,
evaluation a too-large IntLiteral actually yields a ZZ.  This means in
practice that the interpreter never actually creates an object of type
IntLiteral.  The reason this is necessary is because we will otherwise
attempt to use ZZ32 arithmetic on any constant that is too big to fit
in ZZ64!  You might imagine an alternative workaround where we define
redundant math on IntLiterals that yields ZZ, but this will cause all
kinds of problems with the overloading rules as it violates
subtyping.  In practice programmers shouldn't notice this at all (in
stark, stark contrast to the previous bullet).
* A couple of test were invalidated.  XXXextendZZ32.fss doesn't spot
its failure condition (extending a closed trait); it was previously
extending a closed object type and failed as expected.  This has been
filed as a bug.
SpecData/examples/basic/StatPara.Opr.IDENTITYplus.fss appears to have
been fundamentally wrong all along, and we suddenly started spotting
and reporting the bug.  It's been deleted as it was unused in the spec.
```

```
A numeral containing only digits (let $n$ be the number of digits)
has type \EXP{\TYP{NaturalNumeral}\llbracket{}n,10,v\rrbracket} where $v$ is the value of the numeral
interpreted in radix ten.  If the numeral has no leading zeros, or is
the literal \EXP{0}, then it also has type \EXP{\TYP{Literal}\llbracket{}v\rrbracket}.
\note{Can the type \EXP{\TYP{NaturalNumeral}\llbracket{}n, 10, v\rrbracket}
have any value other than what you get from evaluating the corresponding literal?

What is the relationship between \EXP{\TYP{Literal}\llbracket{}v\rrbracket}
and \EXP{\TYP{NaturalNumeral}\llbracket{}n, 10, v\rrbracket}?

We need to describe the \TYP{Numeral} type hierarchy.
All the numeric/numeral types should be defined and their relations to each other given.
And a reference to where that is done should be appear in this section (probably at the beginning of the section).
}

\note{Ought we discuss digit-group separators here?
Or is that just part of lexical structure?
(I think we intend that a numeral consisting of digits and digit-group separators has
type \EXP{\TYP{NaturalNumeral}\llbracket{}n,10,v\rrbracket}
for appropriate values of \VAR{n} and \VAR{v}.)}
```

For example, consider the numeral \EXP{3.1415926535897932384}; converting it immediately to a floating-point number may lose precision. If that numeral is used in an expression involving floating-point intervals, it would be better to convert it directly to an interval. Therefore, numerals have their own types as described above.
